items.question_en: A metal ball initially at pressure of 10⁵ Pa is heated from 20°C to 127°C keeping its volume constant. The coefficient of linear expansion of metal is 10⁻⁵ °C⁻¹ and bulk modulus of metal is 2 × 10¹¹ N/m². The pressure inside the ball becomes

solution.approach: Held at constant volume while heated, the metal is prevented from expanding volumetrically; the bulk modulus converts that blocked volume strain into a pressure rise.

steps.text: Find the volume expansion coefficient from the linear expansion coefficient.
Find the rise in temperature.
The blocked volume strain multiplied by the bulk modulus gives the extra pressure built up.
steps.why_this_step: Bulk modulus is the pressure needed per unit fractional volume change, so it converts the prevented volume expansion directly into pressure.

steps.text: Add the extra pressure to the initial pressure.
steps.why_this_step: The initial pressure of 10⁵ Pa is smaller than the rise by a factor of thousands, so it does not change the rounded answer.

common_mistakes.text: Using the linear expansion coefficient directly as the volume expansion coefficient, without multiplying by 3, gives 2×10⁸ Pa.
Using 2α, the coefficient for area expansion, in place of the volume coefficient 3α gives about 4×10⁸ Pa.

items.question_en: A hole of diameter 5 cm is drilled in a metal sheet at 30 °C. The linear expansion of metal is 2×10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. The diameter of the hole when the temperature is raised to 230 °C, is equal to

solution.approach: A hole in a metal sheet expands like a disc of the same metal, so its diameter grows by the same fraction as any length in the sheet.

steps.text: Write the change in temperature.
Apply linear expansion to the diameter, treating the hole as a disc of the same metal.
steps.why_this_step: Every length in the sheet, including the edge of the hole, scales by the same expansion factor.

steps.text: Evaluate.

common_mistakes.text: Expecting the hole to shrink as the surrounding metal expands inward. Every length in the sheet scales up together, so the hole grows, not shrinks.
Using the area expansion coefficient 2α on the diameter instead of the linear coefficient α gives 5.04 cm.

items.question_en:
Find the ratio of the length of a steel rod and a copper rod if the steel rod is 4 cm longer than the copper rod at any temperature.
[The coefficient of linear expansion for steel and copper are 1.1 × 10⁻⁵/°C and 1.7 × 10⁻⁵/°C respectively]

solution.approach: If the steel rod stays 4 cm longer than the copper rod at every temperature, both rods must expand equally for the same rise, fixing the length ratio.

steps.text: Write the change in length of each rod for the same temperature rise.
steps.equation: ΔL_steel = L_steel α_steel ΔT, ΔL_copper = L_copper α_copper ΔT

steps.text: The 4 cm gap stays fixed at every temperature only if both rods expand by the same amount.
steps.why_this_step: If the two expansions differed, the gap would change as the temperature changed, contradicting the question.

steps.text: Solve for the length ratio.

common_mistakes.text: Inverting the relation and writing L_copper/L_steel instead of L_steel/L_copper gives 11/17.
Mistaking the 4 cm gap as part of the ratio and writing the copper coefficient over 4 gives 17/4.

items.question_en:
An object cools from 100°C to 40°C in 10 minutes, when the surrounding temperature is 10°C. Then the time taken by the object to cool from 70°C to 20°C is
[Take ln 2 = 0.7, ln 3 = 1.1, ln 6 = 1.8]

solution.approach: Newton's law of cooling gives an exponential decay toward the surrounding temperature, so the logarithm of the temperature excess ratio is proportional to time.

steps.text: Write the exponential cooling law with the temperature excess decaying from the surrounding temperature.
Use the first cooling case to find the rate constant k.
Use the second cooling case with the same k to find the unknown time.
steps.why_this_step: The rate constant k depends only on the object and its surroundings, not on the starting temperature, so it carries over from the first case.

steps.text: Solve for t using the value of k found in the first case.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the object cools at a constant rate of 6°C per minute and scaling the 50°C drop proportionally gives about 8.3 min, ignoring that cooling slows near the surrounding temperature.

items.question_en: The heat energy required to convert 10 kg of ice at −10 °C into water at 0 °C is (specific heat capacity of ice = 0.5 cal g⁻¹ and latent heat of fusion of ice = 80 cal g⁻¹)

solution.approach: The heat needed has two parts, first warming the ice to 0°C and then melting it, and the total in calories is converted to joules at the end.

steps.text: Find the heat needed to warm the ice from −10 °C to 0 °C.
steps.equation: Q₁ = mcΔT = 10000 g × 0.5 cal g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ × 10 °C = 50000 cal

steps.text: Find the heat needed to melt all the ice at 0 °C.
steps.equation: Q₂ = mL = 10000 g × 80 cal g⁻¹ = 800000 cal

steps.text: Add the two heats.
Convert the total from calories to joules.
steps.why_this_step: 1 cal = 4.2 J is the conversion used in this exam's calorimetry questions.

common_mistakes.text: Using 10 kg as if it were 1 kg (a misplaced decimal in converting to grams) gives 85000 cal, which is 357 × 10³ J.
Using 10 kg as if it were 100 kg (a misplaced decimal the other way) gives 8500000 cal, which is 357 × 10⁵ J.

items.question_en: When 54 g of ice at −20 °C is mixed with 25 g of steam at 100 °C, then the final mixture at thermal equilibrium contains
options_en: 73 g water at 100 °C and 6 g steam at 100 °C
8 g steam at 100 °C and 12 g water at 0 °C

solution.approach: The heat released by all the steam condensing is compared with the heat needed to melt the ice and warm it to 100°C, fixing how much steam condenses.

steps.text: Find the heat needed to bring all the ice from −20°C to water at 100°C.
Find the heat released if all 25 g of steam condensed at 100°C.
steps.why_this_step: 13500 cal is more than the 10260 cal needed, so not all the steam has to condense; the mixture settles at 100°C.

steps.text: Find the mass of steam that actually condenses to supply exactly the heat needed.
Find the final composition at 100°C.

final_answer.value: 73 g water at 100 °C and 6 g steam at 100 °C

common_mistakes.text: Using the specific heat of ice equal to that of water instead of half that value makes the condensed steam exactly 20 g; mistaking that for the final water forgets the melted ice.
Naively averaging the ice and steam temperatures as (0+100)/2 = 50°C ignores that melting and vaporizing absorb heat before any temperature can rise.

items.question_en: A solid sphere at a temperature T K is cut in to two hemispheres. The ratio of energies radiated by one hemisphere to the whole sphere per second is

solution.approach: Power radiated by a black body is proportional to its exposed surface area, so compare the hemisphere's curved and flat surface to the whole sphere's surface.

steps.text: Write the total surface area of the sphere.
Write the exposed surface area of one hemisphere after the cut, including the flat circular face.
steps.why_this_step: Once the sphere is cut, the flat circular face is no longer touching the other half, so it also radiates.

steps.text: Take the ratio, since radiated power at a fixed temperature is proportional to surface area.

common_mistakes.text: Comparing intensity (power per unit area) instead of total power, which is 1:1 since both surfaces are at the same temperature, ignores that the hemisphere has less total area than the sphere.
Counting only the curved surface of the hemisphere and forgetting the flat circular face exposed by the cut gives 2πr² against 4πr², or 1:2.

items.question_en: A metal metre scale that is accurate up to 0.5 mm is made at a temperature of 25°C. The range of temperatures within which it can be used is (Coefficient of linear expansion of the metal = 10⁻⁵/°C)

solution.approach: The scale reads correctly within the temperature range where the length error caused by expansion or contraction stays within the stated 0.5 mm tolerance.

steps.text: Write the length of the metre scale and the allowed error.
Find the temperature change that produces exactly this length error.
The scale can be used this many degrees above or below the temperature it was made at.
steps.why_this_step: Below the making temperature the metal contracts, making marked lengths too long; above it, the metal expands, making them too short; both directions are limited by the same 0.5 mm tolerance.

common_mistakes.text: Extending the temperature range only above 25°C, from 25°C to 75°C, misses that the scale also misreads by the same amount when cooled below the making temperature.
Treating the 0.5 mm tolerance as split evenly into ±0.25 mm instead of the full 0.5 mm allowed each way gives a narrower range of 0°C to +50°C.
